title: Paramartha Guru Tale 47

full_text:
A wealthy merchant died, bequeathing a chest of copper and silver coins to Guru Paramartha's ashram with the condition that it be distributed to the most deserving, modest poor of the district.

The Guru summoned his disciples: 'We must distribute this treasure with absolute impartiality! According to the sacred scripture: "Let not your right eye see what your left hand gives!" Therefore, to avoid the sin of favoritism, I will distribute the coins while wearing a thick silk blindfold over both eyes!'

The disciples tied three layers of black silk tightly over the Guru's eyes.

The Guru sat upon a stone bench outside the ashram gate with the open chest of coins before him, holding a brass scoop in his hand.

'Announce to the poor that the blindfolded distribution has commenced!' commanded the Guru.

Matti shouted to the road: 'Come, noble poor! Our Guru gives with closed eyes!'

Instead of the modest village poor, three notorious village rascals and pickpockets heard the call. Seeing the old Guru blindfolded with a chest of coins, they smiled with delight.

The first rascal approached, disguised his voice in a squeaky whisper: 'Charity, Master!'

The Guru scooped a handful of silver coins and dropped them into the rascal's cloth: 'May your poverty be healed, son!'

The rascal stepped back, changed his voice to a deep, raspy croak, stepped forward again: 'Charity for an old lame grandmother, Master!'

The Guru dropped another scoop of silver: 'Blessings on your age, grandmother!'

The rascal ran behind a bush, altered his voice to a nasal whine, stepped forward a third time: 'Charity for a blind orphan, Master!'

The Guru scooped more coins: 'Blessings on your youth, orphan!'

For two hours, the same three rascals took turns changing their voices—croaking, wheezing, squeaking, and coughing—collecting sixty scoops of silver and copper coins, filling three heavy gunny sacks!

Meanwhile, an honest, impoverished widow with three hungry children stood timidly at the back of the crowd, too modest to push forward.

When the chest was scraped to the bottom, the Guru removed his blindfold, smiling with saintly satisfaction: 'Behold, my children! We have relieved the distress of sixty distinct, suffering souls without the slightest favoritism!'

At that moment, the widow approached, weeping: 'Master, the three village rascals have taken all the silver, and my starving children have received not a single copper!'

The Guru blinked in dismay: 'Where are the sixty suffering souls?'

Matti pointed down the road: 'There they go, Master! The three rascals are carrying three heavy sacks to the tavern!'

Madayan consoled the Guru: 'Master, your eyes were closed, which preserved your spiritual purity! If the rascals had sixty voices, they suffered from sixty distinct vocal afflictions!'

The Guru emptied his own personal lunch bag, handed his bread to the widow, and vowed: 'Henceforth, we shall open both eyes wide when charity is in our hands!'
moral: Giving charity with closed eyes ensures that rogues take the silver while the needy starve.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Paramartha Guru Tale 47"?
options: Foolishness of book knowledge without worldly wisdom
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

By running away from every problem
